title: Payment connection pool timeouts
executive_summary: INC-012 (SEV2) affected payment-service, with elevated latency and errors and log entries reporting connection pool timeouts, beginning around 10:04-10:06Z on 2026-10-05. The investigation status is ROOT_CAUSE_IDENTIFIED. The leading hypothesis (H1, confidence 0.85, critic-approved) is a configuration regression: change cfg-56d39584 (OPS-2669) reduced payment-service db.pool.max_size from 50 to 10 at 10:04:00Z (cfg-56d39584). A runtime reload record confirms the new cap was applied at the same instant. Pool-acquire timeouts ("Timeout acquiring connection from pool payment-db-pool after 5000ms", active=10, idle=0) first appear at 10:06:13Z, 29 times through 10:34:18Z (logpat-payment-service-7d1739af). Payment timeout rate rose from a baseline of 0.1 to a window mean of 6.3, and error rate from 0.8 to 9.17 (met-payment-service-timeout_rate-0940-1035, met-payment-service-error_rate-0940-1035). Request rate was flat (about 300 req/s), so the change in capacity, not a change in load, is the most probable explanation. This is not a confirmed fact. The symptoms resemble last year's pool exhaustion, but the evidence points away from a database-side cause (H3 rejected). The mechanism is consistent with the observed data, not independently proven at every instance.

hypotheses.description: Config change cfg-56d39584 (OPS-2669) reduced payment-service db.pool.max_size from 50 to 10 at 10:04Z, starving the payment-db-pool under normal load and causing pool-acquire timeouts, errors and timeouts. Mechanism: max_size cut 50->10 (80% reduction) -> pool active pinned at 10 with idle=0 -> requests queue for connections -> acquire waits hit the 5000ms timeout -> ERROR 'Timeout acquiring connection' logs, timeout_rate ~0.1%->~12%, error_rate ~0.8%->~17%. The same cap explains the postgres-side connection utilisation falling ~22% from 10:07: payment-service now holds at most 10 DB connections instead of up to 50. Request rate is flat, so the reduced capacity alone is sufficient without any load change.

hypotheses.description: A pool-internal fault, such as connection leak or long-held connections (for example a stuck transaction or missing release in the payment code path), exhausted the pool. The 50->10 change is coincident, or merely exposed the problem. Mechanism: Connections are acquired and not returned, or held for long periods, so the pool fills regardless of DB-side load -> active pinned at max -> waiting queue grows -> acquire timeouts. The DB-side connection count falls because the leaked connections are held in the app, not executing queries, so DB load stays flat.

critic_review.summary: H1 is well supported. The config change cfg-56d39584 (db.pool.max_size 50->10, OPS-2669) is confirmed at 10:04:00Z, and a runtime 'Configuration reloaded: db.pool.max_size=10 (version 77)' INFO log appears at the same instant, so the cap was applied at runtime. Pool-acquire timeout logs (active=10, idle=0, growing waiters) start at 10:06:13Z, and payment error and timeout rates step up at 10:06. Pool utilisation rises from 10:05. Request rate is flat (300->299 req/s), there is no deployment in the window, and the only payment-service config change in 09:00-10:40 is this one. Postgres latency, CPU and disk IO are flat, which rules out a DB-side saturation story. The 1-minute lead of pool utilisation over the error onset is a minor sampling detail. Limitations: the per-instance effective value was not checked beyond the reload log, and the log count in the summary (14 pattern matches vs 29 quoted) is a minor inconsistency that does not change the conclusion.

assessments.reasoning: Config change at 10:04:00Z is confirmed by both the change record and a runtime reload log at the same time. Timeouts start at 10:06 with the capped-pool signature (active=10, idle=0, waiting queue growing). Request rate is flat and no deployment or other config change is present, so reduced capacity is the most parsimonious cause. DB-side metrics are healthy.

A leak would not explain the sudden onset at 10:06, which lines up with the cap cut. No leak-specific evidence was found, and the 50-cap pool was not shown to be saturating before 10:04. The cut alone is sufficient, so a leak is at most a secondary contributor that is not supported by the data.
Postgres p99 latency (25.1ms vs 25.2ms), CPU (35%), and disk IO wait are flat, and Postgres connection utilisation falls about 23%. This contradicts a DB-side slowdown holding connections longer.

Payment request rate is flat (-0.4%), gateway and order-service request rates are flat, and there is no order-service timeout increase. There is no sign of a traffic amplification or retry storm reaching payment-service.

root_cause_statement: ROOT CAUSE IDENTIFIED (critic-approved; still an INFERENCE from evidence): configuration_regression in payment-service - Config change cfg-56d39584 (OPS-2669) reduced payment-service db.pool.max_size from 50 to 10 at 10:04Z, starving the payment-db-pool under normal load and causing pool-acquire timeouts, errors and timeouts.
corrective_actions: Revert db.pool.max_size on payment-service from 10 to 50 (rollback of cfg-56d39584 / OPS-2669), and confirm the reload log shows the restored value on all instances.
Verify per-instance effective pool size on every payment-service instance, since only one reload record was observed (cfg-56d39584).
Confirm recovery: payment timeout_rate and error_rate return to baseline (about 0.1% and 0.8%) and pool-acquire timeout logs stop.
preventive_actions: Require review and a load-test or capacity check for any change to database pool sizing, and flag reductions above a set threshold (for example, an 80% cut) for approval.
Add config-change validation that compares pool settings with the previous value and with expected concurrency before rollout.
Record the ticket-to-change link (OPS-2669) in the change log so that config changes are auditable against incidents.
Investigate the unresolved possibility of a connection leak or long-held connections in the payment code path (H2), so that a future reduction in pool size does not cause an outage on its own.
monitoring_recommendations: Alert on payment-db-pool active/max ratio sustained at or near 100% with idle=0 and waiting > 0 for more than 2 minutes.
Alert on 'Timeout acquiring connection' log rate above zero for payment-service, and on payment timeout_rate and error_rate exceeding baseline by a set margin.
Emit and dashboard the effective db.pool.max_size per instance at each config reload, and alert on any value change outside a change window.
Track payment request rate alongside pool utilisation so that capacity-driven saturation can be distinguished from load-driven saturation.
Monitor postgres connection counts from payment-service and p99 latency to detect any future database-side contribution.
limitations: Only one runtime reload record was observed; the effective value on each payment-service instance was not independently verified.
The connection-leak or long-held-connection hypothesis (H2) was not excluded by the data, though it is not needed to explain the onset.
Flat p99 latency during the incident may partly reflect failed requests being excluded from the measure; this was assumed, not verified.
The pool utilisation metric leads error onset by about one minute; this is treated as a sampling detail.
Callers' retry configuration (api-gateway, order-service) could not be checked; traffic amplification was rejected based on flat request rates.

conclusion: The most probable root cause of INC-012 is the reduction of payment-service db.pool.max_size from 50 to 10 by change cfg-56d39584 (OPS-2669) at 10:04Z. With request rate flat, the reduced pool capacity alone is sufficient to explain the pool-acquire timeouts, elevated error and timeout rates, and the lower postgres connection utilisation. Database-side saturation and traffic surge were ruled out by the telemetry. Remaining uncertainties are whether every instance received the new value and whether a latent connection-holding issue exists in the payment code path. Reverting the change is the primary mitigation, and the preventive and monitoring actions aim to prevent a recurrence.
